newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria may lose out on gas transit - Topenergy.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria may lose out on gas transit - Topenergy.

text.p: Bulgarian-Russian joint stock company Topenergy said it wants a quick decision from Sofia on a concession for transiting Russian gas through Bulgaria as Russia is already looking at alternative pipeline routes.

Topenergy board member Nikolay Valkanov confirmed on Thursday that Russian gas monopoly RAO Gazprom, which holds 50 percent in the joint company, had decided to build a pipeline under the Black Sea to supply Russian gas to Turkey.

"Apart from Gazprom, Turkey also is interested in receiving Russian gas supplies and wants to solve its energy problem," Valkanov told Reuters in an interview. "Serbia is also looking for ways to receive gas supplies," he said.
Valkanov said the Bulgarian government should decide quickly whether to grant a concession to Topenergy as otherwise Bulgaria might miss its chance.

"There is no time left. A decision should be taken as soon as possible. It is a matter of days," Valkanov said, adding that Bulgaria could make a profit of $100 million per year for allowing gas to transit through its territory.
Topenergy, which was established by Gazprom and Bulgarian state-owned Bulgargas in 1995, last May applied for a concession to build new pipelines in Bulgaria.
"Topenergy needs a concession of 30 or 50 years as enlarging the gas transiting system on Bulgarian territory is expected to cost some $500 million," Valkanov said.
The company plans to carry Russian natural gas through Romania. From Bulgaria it will be distributed to Turkey, Greece, Macedonia and Serbia.
Valkanov said that because of its geographical position Bulgaria could become an energy centre for the Balkans.
Bulgaria has a 2,200-km pipeline network, including 625 km of transit pipelines which receive and transmit gas from outside the country.
Bulgaria supplies Turkey with three billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas per year and started supplying some gas to Greece last month.

Sofia has built a pipeline to Macedonia and is waiting for its western neighbour to complete construction work on its territory and start gas supplies. Bulgargas has plans to build a pipeline to Serbia.
Topenergy has said it needs to enlarge the transit pipeline network to 1,300 km by 2010 and build 240-megawatt compressor stations to meet the growing Balkan demand.

The firm plans to increase the Bulgarian distribution system from 17 bcm to some 30 bcm. It envisages annual supplies of Russian gas in 2010 of 20 bcm for Turkey, four bcm for Greece, one bcm for Albania, two bcm for Serbia and one bcm for Macedonia.

Bulgarian newspapers quoted Alexander Avdeev, Russia's ambassador in Sofia, as Russia had promised gas supplies to other countries and would be looking for alternative pipeline routes at the beginning of 1997.
